title: The list that saves you money before you leave home
description: The cheapest shopping trip is the one planned at the kitchen table. How a proper list — built from your shelves, not your cravings — quietly cuts the bill.

body.heading: Start from the shelves, not the shop
paragraphs: Most lists are written from memory and appetite, which is why homes contain three jars of the same spice and no pasta. Build the list the other way round: look in the cupboard, fridge and freezer first, plan meals around what is already there, and list only the gaps.
This one habit attacks the two biggest leaks at once — buying duplicates, and letting food you already paid for expire quietly at the back of a shelf.

body.heading: Write it like you mean it
paragraphs: Group the list by the shop's layout — produce, dairy, tins, frozen — so you walk each aisle once and are not led back past the tempting displays. Put quantities on it: “2 onions” is a plan; “onions” is an invitation.
Add one deliberate treat line. A list with a treat on it is a list you will keep; a list of pure virtue usually survives until the biscuit aisle.

body.heading: The rule that makes it work
paragraphs: In the shop, the rule is simple: if it is not on the list, it needs a reason out loud. Not a ban — a reason. “We are out of it at home” is a reason. “It looked nice” is information about the display designer, not about your needs.
Keep the lists for a month and read them together. They are the truest record of what your household actually eats — and the best foundation any food budget can have.

takeaway: Build the list from your shelves, group it by aisle, add quantities and one honest treat — then let anything unlisted argue its case out loud.
